item.title: Tiburon Peninsula under evacuation advisory as Thanksgiving king tides near
item.description: The entire Tiburon Peninsula is under a Level 1 evacuation advisory ahead of the Nov. 24-26 king tides, which could push the bay to 8-9 feet. Residents are urged to prepare now.
item.content:encoded:
The entire Tiburon Peninsula is under a Level 1 evacuation advisory ahead of the Nov. 24-26 king tides, which could push the bay to 8-9 feet. Residents are urged to prepare now.

The entire Tiburon Peninsula is under an evacuation advisory ahead of the Nov. 24-26 king tides, which Tiburon public works staff expect to push the bay to 8-9 feet at the Nov. 25 peak — about where it stood in the floods of 1982-1983.

The Level 1 advisory, issued through AlertMarin, is the lowest of three levels, meant to give residents notice and time to prepare rather than to order anyone out. A warning would tell residents to be ready to leave and to consider going early; an order would mean leaving immediately.

Still, officials are urging people in low-lying neighborhoods not to wait.

In an AlertMarin message sent at 5:02 p.m. Nov. 19, the Tiburon and Southern Marin fire protection districts warned of “historic high tides” Nov. 22-27 and urged residents of low-lying areas to secure their property and consider leaving before each day’s late-morning high tide. Storms could push the water even higher than the forecast, Tiburon said.

The worry is getting on and off the peninsula. If Tiburon Boulevard and Paradise Drive flood on the same tide, travel in and out could be very limited, Patrick Kerslake, Tiburon’s public works operations and technology manager, told the Town Council Nov. 18. In Belvedere, flooding on San Rafael Avenue and Beach Road, the city’s only two roads in and out, could temporarily cut off the community and restrict emergency vehicle access, the city has warned.

Officials are also urging residents to stay off flooded roads and be ready to shelter in place or leave through the Thanksgiving weekend.

Tiburon, Belvedere, both police departments and both fire districts will add staff from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Kerslake said. A storm could bring 1-3 inches of rain to the North Bay on Nov. 24-25, the first days of the king tides, though the National Weather Service said Nov. 19 that the timing is still uncertain. The weather service expects to upgrade its coastal flood advisory for the bays to a coastal flood warning as the king tides approach.

The peninsula got a look at what rain and a high tide can do together Nov. 18, when almost 3 inches of rain fell on the peninsula, Kerslake told the council.

At Tiburon Boulevard and Beach Road, water still covered the intersection about 10 a.m. that day, some three hours after the 7:13 a.m. high tide NOAA predicted at Point Chauncey, its prediction station for Tiburon and Belvedere. Rogelio Valdez, a maintenance worker with the town’s Department of Public Works, waded through the water, setting cones to steer drivers toward the shallowest water.

Two things flooded the intersection, Kerslake said: the receding high tide and rainwater trapped in the storm drains. Those drains empty into the bay through a flap gate, a one-way valve at the outfall.

“Until the tide levels recede, the flap gate will not open and allow water from the stormwater system to drain into the bay via gravity,” he said.

Water also pooled in the Blackie’s Pasture parking lot and at Tiburon Boulevard’s intersections with San Rafael Avenue and with Gilmartin Drive, Kerslake said. A Tiburon police truck blocked the entrance to the Blackie’s Pasture lot that morning.

“Not all were tidally influenced but some were likely related to the combination of very high rainfall intensity and higher-than-predicted astronomical water levels in (San Francisco Bay)/Richardson Bay,” he said.

Water covered The Boardwalk shopping center parking lot in downtown Tiburon. Minor flooding also covered part of Greenwood Cove Drive near the 76 station and The Cove at Tiburon apartments, where a portable pump and a wall of sandbags were in place. In Belvedere, Cove Road flooded and was closed between Lagoon Road and Beach Road, with signs at both ends.

The water also shut down Belvedere Nursery School at 15 Cove Road Place. It began entering classrooms about 9:30 a.m. Nov. 18, and soon 2 inches of water stood inside, said Abigail Vare, executive director of Belvedere-Hawthorne Nursery Schools. Staff had brought in sandbags lined with plastic and kept a sump pump on site, said Gindin Meuse, the schools’ operations manager.

The building is closed indefinitely. The school plans to move its 60 students to its Hawthorne Pre-K campus at 145 Rock Hill Road in Tiburon after Thanksgiving break, pending state licensing, Vare said. Meuse said repairs will have to wait until the wet season’s king tides pass.

King tides are the year’s highest astronomical tides. NOAA predicts this round will peak at 7.03 feet above the average daily low tide at 10:49 a.m. Nov. 25 at its San Francisco gauge, the figure Belvedere is using. At Point Chauncey, NOAA predicts high tides of 6.8 feet at 10:33 a.m. 24, 6.89 feet at 11:17 a.m. 25 and 6.81 feet at 12:06 p.m. 26.

Those predictions don’t account for weather or for warmer-than-normal ocean water, which the weather service says is adding to tidal flooding around the bay. NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center said Nov. 12 that El Niño is still strengthening, with greater than 79% odds that a strong to very strong event lasts through January-March.

Water has been running 1-2 feet above predictions fairly consistently, which would put the king tides at 8.1-9.2 feet, Kerslake told the council. In the 48 hours through Nov. 19, during a storm, water ran about 1.6 feet above predictions. If that held, the Nov. 24-26 tides would reach about 8.4-8.5 feet at Point Chauncey, by Ark estimates based on NOAA predictions and gauge readings.

Belvedere staff projected 8.6 feet this month without storm surge, against low points of about 8 feet along San Rafael Avenue and Beach Road, by the city’s measure. NOAA’s San Francisco gauge recorded its highest water level, 8.66 feet, in January 1983, the same level Kerslake cited for Richardson Bay during those floods.

The tides climb each day before the Nov. 25 peak. The weather service’s coastal flood advisory runs until 11 a.m. Nov. 21. It expects the 8:15 a.m. high tide that day to reach 7.2 feet at the San Francisco gauge, 1.4 feet above normal. At Point Chauncey, NOAA predicts 5.9 feet at 8:43 a.m. 21, 6.27 feet at 9:16 a.m. 22 and 6.58 feet at 9:53 a.m. 23. By Ark estimates, every daytime high tide from Nov. 21 through Nov. 28 could reach levels that have flooded Greenwood Cove Drive and Tiburon Boulevard at Beach Road.

Kerslake said residents should watch the whole week until the tides recede. More king tides are due Dec. 23-25, over Christmas, and Jan. 21-22. NOAA predicts the Dec. 24 tide will run slightly higher than the November peak, at 7.09 feet at Point Chauncey.

Kerslake listed the low spots that control access to the peninsula: Tiburon Boulevard, which Caltrans maintains as Highway 131, at Greenwood Cove Drive, at Blackie’s Pasture Road and at Beach Road; the San Rafael Avenue and Beach Road entries into Belvedere; and Paradise Drive at Robin Drive, just outside town limits toward Corte Madera.

During peak tides, sheltering in place may be safer than driving for residents outside flood-prone areas, Kerslake said.

Steven Torrence, director of the county Office of Emergency Management, said in October that the county would send AlertMarin warnings ahead of any tide predicted to reach about 7 feet, roughly where water starts reaching Highway 101.

Golden Gate Ferry, which serves Tiburon, said Nov. 20 that forecast strong winds and higher-than-usual tides could lead it to suspend Tiburon and Larkspur service Nov. 24 and could bring boarding-gate changes and delays at Larkspur and San Francisco on Nov. 23, 25 and 27. It runs no boats Nov. 26, Thanksgiving Day, and a weekend schedule Nov. 27. Golden Gate Transit buses run weekend schedules both days.

At the Nov. 18 meeting, Councilmember Holli Thier said residents were asking whether and when they could drive to the East Bay or San Francisco for Thanksgiving. She suggested the town address holiday travel in its Tiburon Talk newsletter.

Staff from the peninsula’s agencies have been meeting weekly to plan for the winter and check in daily or more often during storms, Kerslake said.

The town has posted programmable message boards at its entry and exit points and has rented more to deploy as needed. At the Nov. 18 meeting, Councilmember Jack Ryan said some message boards along Tiburon Boulevard were still displaying a Nov. 2 date. Kerslake said those belong to the contractor on a Caltrans maintenance project and that the town was already working on it.

Crews are stocking community resource centers and setting up more sites with partners across the peninsula, he said. The town is tracking its costs in case state and federal disaster reimbursement becomes available.

Tiburon and Belvedere share an emergency operations center at the Tiburon Police Department, which Town Manager Greg Chanis said in October would be set up but not staffed during king tides and forecast storms. Each of the six or seven traffic signals on Tiburon Boulevard can run on its own generator if the power goes out, Chanis said. Kerslake said in October that Town Hall will be a community resource center.

Since early November, public works crews have set wooden tide boxes, sealed and weighted with bags, over storm drains at Tiburon Boulevard and Beach Road, at Beach Road and Juanita Lane, and in other low spots. The boxes hold bay water rising through the drains instead of letting it spill onto the street, a technique Mayor Jon Welner praised Nov. 18 at his last council meeting. Crews remove them when it rains because the drains have to carry runoff, and depending on rain and the tide, residents should then expect flooding in those areas, the town said.

“The town’s new pump would be unable to keep up with the volume of water at this location,” Kerslake said of the Beach Road intersection.

Town staff will watch the intersection and close it if the water makes the road impassable, he said.

Tiburon Fire Protection District crews will answer life-threatening calls first during storms, so help with minor flooding, downed trees and debris may be delayed, the district said in October.

“We will be more proactive than ever to keep firefighters on duty during predicted storm patterns and king tides,” Fire Chief Tommy Hellyer said.

The Southern Marin Fire Protection District, which covers Strawberry and Tiburon west of Trestle Glen Boulevard, also planned to add staff based on the expected hazards.

“We’ll posture and scale for the response,” Battalion Chief Jon Butler said in October.

In a Nov. 19 advisory, Belvedere warned residents that water could run well above predicted tides and urged them to prepare.

On Oct. 28, a tide predicted at 6.7 feet reached a reported 8.2 feet at San Rafael Avenue, overtopping the lowest stretches of shoreline without a storm, according to the advisory. On Nov. 13, a coastal storm pushed water close to 8 feet on a predicted tide of 5.5 feet.

The City Council declared a local emergency Nov. 9 and approved up to $180,000 for flood protection.

“Waiting until roads are flooded could substantially limit our options,” City Manager Robert Zadnik told the council.

The city has ordered 2,000 feet of a 16-inch-high Geodesign barrier, built of metal supports, panels and a waterproof membrane, for the San Rafael Avenue waterfront path. It expects the barrier to raise protection at the lowest points from about 8 to 9.3 feet. The path will likely stay closed for the rest of the king-tide season, and the city asks pedestrians to use the sidewalk on the opposite side.

City staff had first recommended a NOAQ Boxwall barrier for San Rafael Avenue but chose Geodesign after weighing wind exposure, anchoring and performance in coastal storms. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has tested the Geodesign barrier, which is better suited to waves and storm surge, the city said.

On Beach Road, the city plans removable panels near the China Cabin, sandbags at vulnerable openings and temporary storm-drain plugs. On Cove Road, it plans a temporary NOAQ Boxwall barrier to keep water flowing downhill from downtown Tiburon off the road, and public works crews have staged sandbags and a pump there. The city aims to have all of its barriers in place by Nov. 22, depending on deliveries, field conditions and assembly. It will reassess them after the November king tides.

The barriers are going up while the city’s Beach Road seawall project is still underway. Public Works Director Antony Boyd told the project’s oversight subcommittee Nov. 17 that the contractor’s Dec. 4 completion date is unlikely and the work will probably run until at least mid-December.

Most of the construction zone sits behind a solid concrete wall, Boyd said. The city plans barriers at the gangway entrances and other openings in the wall, working with the Belvedere Land Co. It also plans an inflatable plug in a storm drain between the buildings over the water and Main Street.

Depending on rain and the tide, crews may have to unplug the Beach Road drains to let rainwater out, Boyd said. The flap gates on those drains were not part of the seawall project, and staff told the subcommittee they are reviewing the gates’ condition and weighing a stopgap in the meantime.

The Belvedere Lagoon Property Owners Association has lowered the lagoon to its winter operating level, tested its pumps and weir gates, and arranged for backup generators and on-call crews, the city said.

The barriers protect public roads, not private homes, and they could be overtopped, the city said, urging residents to protect their own property.

The advisory could escalate depending on the weather and flooding, the city said. It asked residents near the lagoon, West Shore Road, Beach Road, Cove Road and San Rafael Avenue to watch conditions and consider leaving early rather than wait for roads to flood. It suggested that those in low-lying areas with flexible Thanksgiving plans consider spending the holiday elsewhere.

If an evacuation is needed, residents could be directed to collection points that may include the Belvedere Community Center, St. Stephen’s Episcopal Church in Belvedere and Tiburon Town Hall. Belvedere police offer evacuation tags residents can display once everyone has left a home, so responders know which properties still need checks.

City staff will be on call through each king tide period and will report to work ahead of the highest tides if needed, before flooding can cut off access to Belvedere, the city said. Block captains may help run the collection points.

To free up higher ground for cars, the city suspended its 72-hour parking limit Nov. 19, though all other parking rules still apply.

The county had planned such measures for Greenwood Cove Drive. Judd Goodman, a Marin County senior civil engineer and the staff liaison to Marin County Flood Control District Zone 4, said in October that sandbag walls would go up along the drive ahead of the king tides expected around Thanksgiving, backed by check valves and inflatable plugs. He also said a 6-inch portable pump for emergencies was expected by mid-November.

The county also planned quick-build barriers by the gas station near Greenwood Cove Drive, where tides spill onto Tiburon Boulevard, to protect the boulevard’s inbound lanes and possibly the drive itself, Kerslake told the council in October. County public works officials did not respond to a request for comment.

In Strawberry, the county, Caltrans and Mill Valley have been working on sandbags, valves on drainage culverts and temporary barriers to reduce flooding at the Seminary Drive exit from Highway 101, county spokesperson Anastasia Pallas said in October. King tides caused most of last winter’s flooding there, she said.

Sign up for AlertMarin, at alertmarin.org, to get emergency alerts by call, text or email for your address. Tiburon also suggests opting in to AlertMarin’s Coastal Flooding and King Tides alerts. Fewer than half of county residents have registered, Emergency Preparedness Council Chair Tom Cromwell said in October. Belvedere also urges residents to look up their evacuation zone on Genasys Protect, at protect.genasys.com.

Be ready to shelter in place or leave. Kerslake urged residents to pack stay-at-home kits and go bags, stay away from the shoreline and seawalls at high tide, and check on neighbors who are older or may need help.

Move vehicles to higher ground and move valuables, documents and electronics off ground floors and garage floors, Tiburon advises. Expect road closures near the shoreline during high tides.

Never walk or drive through water of unknown depth, the town said, citing the National Weather Service: One foot of water can carry away most cars, and 2 feet can carry away SUVs and trucks.

Free sandbag stations are at Blackie’s Pasture and at Teather Park behind CVS in Tiburon. Kerslake said in October that the Tiburon stations are open around the clock but that residents must fill their own bags. The town recommends sandbags around doors, garages and other low entry points in flood-prone areas.

In Belvedere, free sandbags are on Community Road across from City Hall, at Lagoon Road and Maybridge Road, on West Shore Road across from No. 71, and at a higher-capacity self-service station in the Lagoon Road parking lot, though supplies may be limited. For Strawberry and Alto residents, the Southern Marin Fire Protection District lists a station at 10 Milland Drive, next to the fire road gate. Belvedere recommends buying sandbags from a hardware store well ahead of a storm or king tide.

Clear leaves from gutters, storm drains and driveways and put them in the green bin rather than the street, Tiburon advises. It also recommends trimming branches and securing outdoor furniture.

Salt water can seep into the lithium-ion batteries of electric cars, e-bikes and scooters and spark a fire hours or days later, often after they are parked in a garage, Belvedere warned. Never drive or ride them through salt water, and move e-bikes, scooters and chargers off garage floors before high tides, the city said.

The county’s Public Emergency Portal, at emergency.marincounty.gov, maps road closures, storm hazards, power outages and evacuations with information from agencies across Marin. Tiburon’s El Niño resources are at townoftiburon.gov/elnino, and SNAP Radio, at 840 AM, is the peninsula’s emergency station. The Tiburon Talk and Belvedere Breeze newsletters carry local updates; sign up for Tiburon Talk at townoftiburon.gov/newsletter.

To report a drainage problem on public property in Tiburon, call Public Works at 415-435-7399 or Tiburon police at 415-789-2800 after hours. For road flooding or barrier problems in Belvedere, call Belvedere police at 415-435-3266. Belvedere City Hall, at 415-435-3838, takes general questions during business hours. In Strawberry and other unincorporated areas, report flooded roads to the county through FixItMarin, online or by app. Call 911 for immediate danger.

The Beach Road intersection’s flap gate is due for replacement. Engineering Manager David Eshoo told the council in September that the gate doesn’t seal, letting the tide back up into the intersection. He also said the town’s storm-drain relining wouldn’t fix the flooding there; a pump station would, at a cost of millions. But a contractor certified to work in confined spaces, hired after a high tide flooded the intersection without rain Oct. 11, found the gate in working condition, Kerslake said.

The relining has started and is focused on corrugated metal pipe around town, he said.

A trash-capture project Eshoo is designing will reroute drainage at the intersection and replace the flap gate, Kerslake said. The town’s design consultant is also studying whether the town could add equipment to pump water around the gate at high tide, as the Belvedere Lagoon is pumped down.

Town staff told the council in September that the trash-capture project would be built in summer 2027 with a Caltrans grant of about $600,000 once Caltrans issues a permit.

item.title: Family, friends honor Belvedere girl Harper Tan’s memory
item.description: Harper Tan, a 7-year-old Belvedere girl, died July 28 of a rare brain cancer. A bench at the new Artist’s View deck will bear her name, and her family set up the Harper Tan Memorial Library Fund at Reed and Harper’s Light Foundation.
item.content:encoded:
Harper Tan, a 7-year-old Belvedere girl, died July 28 of a rare brain cancer. A bench at the new Artist’s View deck will bear her name, and her family set up the Harper Tan Memorial Library Fund at Reed and Harper’s Light Foundation.

Belvedere 7-year-old Harper Tan cheered on her sunflower every day, talked her father out of killing spiders and, at 3½, announced plans to build houses for people living in tents.

Harper, who was about to start second grade at Reed Elementary School, died July 28 of a rare brain cancer. She painted for hours, made friends instantly and, on every birthday and every dandelion, wished for a lot of Cheetos.

Now a bench with her name will sit at the new Artist’s View deck, a lookout her family often passed on their walks. The Belvedere Parks, Open Spaces and Lanes Committee approved it Nov. 3. Donors also have given more than $21,000 to a library fund her family set up at Reed, the Harper Tan Memorial Library Fund, and her parents have started Harper’s Light Foundation to spread the kindness she showed.

item.title: Belvedere rejects Mallard Pointe permit appeal after four-hour hearing
item.description: The Belvedere City Council unanimously rejected a residents group’s appeal of Mallard Pointe’s bulkhead permits Nov. 9, finding paperwork errors but no reason to overturn them.
item.content:encoded:
The Belvedere City Council unanimously rejected a residents group’s appeal of Mallard Pointe’s bulkhead permits Nov. 9, finding paperwork errors but no reason to overturn them.

The Belvedere City Council unanimously rejected a residents group’s challenge to Mallard Pointe’s bulkhead permits Nov. 9, ending a heavily attended four-hour afternoon hearing in which members acknowledged paperwork errors but found no basis to overturn the approvals.

The council first voted 4-1 to deny a request by Belvedere Residents for Intelligent Growth, or BRIG, to postpone the hearing, with Councilmember Jane Cooper dissenting. BRIG wanted to keep the appeal open through the winter, arguing the rains of a predicted El Niño season would show how construction along the lagoon shoreline was holding up.

All five members then voted to deny the appeal, leaving intact two permits issued Oct. 1 to replace about 900 feet of shoreline bulkheads. The work includes removing the old walls, driving vinyl sheet piles into the lagoon bed and excavating and backfilling behind them.

item.title: Belvedere declares flood emergency, authorizes $180,000 for winter preparations
item.description: Belvedere plans to line up to 1,800 feet of the San Rafael Avenue bayside path with 20-inch flood barriers under a $180,000 plan the City Council approved Nov. 9.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere plans to line up to 1,800 feet of the San Rafael Avenue bayside path with 20-inch flood barriers under a $180,000 plan the City Council approved Nov. 9.

Belvedere plans to line up to 1,800 feet of the bayside path along San Rafael Avenue with 20-inch plastic flood barriers and close the path for much of the winter under a $180,000 plan the City Council approved Nov. 9.

The move came with the council’s declaration of local emergency ahead of unusually high tides expected around Thanksgiving, Christmas and in January, letting city officials speed up emergency purchases. On Beach Road, the plan would close gaps in the seawall railing with panels, sandbag gangways and plug storm drains.

Councilmembers approved the money but left the details to staff. They directed Public Works Director Antony Boyd to gather more information about how well the barriers would work and to settle the final approach with Mayor Sally Wilkinson and Vice Mayor Kevin Burke.

item.title: Crystal Duran leaving Belvedere-Tiburon Library to become Santa Clara city librarian
item.description: Belvedere-Tiburon Library Director Crystal Duran will become Santa Clara’s city librarian Dec. 14. Her last day in Tiburon is Dec. 5, and Joey Della Santina will serve as interim director.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere-Tiburon Library Director Crystal Duran will become Santa Clara’s city librarian Dec. 14. Her last day in Tiburon is Dec. 5, and Joey Della Santina will serve as interim director.

This story was updated Nov. 17 after the city of Santa Clara announced Duran’s appointment, following The Ark’s deadline for its Nov. 18 print edition.

Belvedere-Tiburon Library Director Crystal Duran is leaving her post after nearly five years on the job to become Santa Clara’s city librarian.

The city of Santa Clara announced the appointment Nov. 17. Duran starts there Dec. 14, succeeding City Librarian Patty Wong, who is retiring, and was chosen after a nationwide search that included interviews with the city’s Board of Library Trustees and city staff, the city said.

Duran’s last day at the Belvedere-Tiburon Library is Dec. 5. Assistant Director for Library Service Joey Della Santina will serve as interim director beginning Dec. 6.

The Library Agency board unanimously appointed Della Santina to the interim role in closed session at a special meeting Nov. 12. He will have the support of an outside adviser while he serves as interim.

item.description: Santa photos, a downtown Tiburon festival and Hanukkah celebrations return to the peninsula next month.
item.content:encoded:
Santa photos, a downtown Tiburon festival and Hanukkah celebrations return to the peninsula next month.

Santa photos, a downtown Tiburon festival and Hanukkah celebrations return to the peninsula next month along with a pop-up drive collecting donations for Bay Area nonprofits.

The Tiburon Peninsula Chamber of Commerce’s annual holiday festival headlines the event slate when it returns 2-5 p.m. Dec. 5 in downtown Tiburon. Lower Main Street will be closed to car traffic from noon to 6 p.m. that day.

Chamber Executive Director Melanie Haddad said in an email the event showcases how the town “is such a magical place during the holidays, with the festive lights and beautiful waterfront views.”

item.title: Belvedere pares back initial police review, defers analysis of alternatives
item.description: Belvedere will pay a consultant up to $97,985 to assess whether its seven-person police force is staffed and funded to last.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere will pay a consultant up to $97,985 to assess whether its seven-person police force is staffed and funded to last.

Belvedere will pay a consultant up to $97,985 to assess whether its seven-person police force is staffed and funded to last after years of trouble covering shifts.

The City Council unanimously approved the contract with MRG, an Elk Grove-based consulting firm formerly known as Municipal Resource Group, on Nov. 9. The first phase will examine staffing, supervision, deployment, workload and coverage during vacancies and turnover, along with the department’s financial sustainability over five- and 10-year periods. Any detailed study of alternatives, such as a merger with the Tiburon Police Department, would need a separate council vote and its own money in the 2027-2028 budget. MRG estimates that work at $20,000 to $125,000, depending on how many options the council wants studied.

Two firms answered the city’s July request for proposals: MRG, at $120,396, and Raftelis, at $123,858, each about four times the $30,000 the city had budgeted. The original request sought both an assessment of the department and a review of alternative ways to deliver police services, City Manager Robert Zadnik said. At the city’s request, MRG narrowed its proposal to start with the current department, and its price for that first phase fell to $87,985. A $10,000 contingency, which the city manager must approve in advance and in writing, brings the total to $97,985.

item.title: Strawberry Rec delays playground approval pending construction bids
item.description: The Strawberry Recreation District put the site work for its new playground out to bid and held off approving the playground equipment.
item.content:encoded:
The Strawberry Recreation District put the site work for its new playground out to bid and held off approving the playground equipment.

The Strawberry Recreation District has put the site work for its new playground out to bid and held off approving the playground equipment until it has a contractor for that work.

The board voted 4-0 Nov. 10, with board member Sarah Waterfield absent, to seek bids for foundational work such as excavation and a retaining wall. Playground company GameTime will design the playground and install its equipment.

The board delayed a vote on GameTime’s playground design until the district secures a site-work contractor. GameTime’s sales manager told the board the order must be placed by Nov. 30 to guarantee the price. The district may ask the company to extend the deadline until the board’s Dec. 8 meeting. If that request is denied, the board may call a special meeting Nov. 30.

item.title: Del Mar students bring their artwork to Tiburon Town Hall
item.description: Work by Del Mar Middle School’s intermediate and advanced art students hangs at Tiburon Town Hall from Nov. 23 through Dec. 23, with an artists’ reception Dec. 1.
item.content:encoded:
Work by Del Mar Middle School’s intermediate and advanced art students hangs at Tiburon Town Hall from Nov. 23 through Dec. 23, with an artists’ reception Dec. 1.

Eighth grader Mila Schoen painted her dog because, she says, French bulldogs look silly. Seventh grader Antonio De Mendonca Neto built a Nike high-top out of paper and glue without looking at a picture.

Both pieces will hang at Tiburon Town Hall from Nov. 23 through Dec. 23 in a show of work by Del Mar Middle School’s intermediate and advanced art students. An artists’ reception is set for 6-8 p.m. Dec. 1.

item.title: Library show ‘Palette in Play’ explores how artists use color
item.description: The Belvedere-Tiburon Library’s next art show, “Palette in Play: How Artists Use Color,” opens Nov. 19 with an artists’ reception and runs through Jan. 13.
item.content:encoded:
The Belvedere-Tiburon Library’s next art show, “Palette in Play: How Artists Use Color,” opens Nov. 19 with an artists’ reception and runs through Jan. 13.

Pete Pedersen started drawing on the backs of blueprints. As boys, he and his brothers spent hours sketching on the big sheets their parents, who ran an architecture firm, threw away.

He went to public schools in Tiburon, grew up to be a landscape architect and designed the landscaping plan for the Old Rail Trail beside Tiburon Boulevard, completed in 1992. Now one of his oil paintings, “Somewhere South,” is part of “Palette in Play: How Artists Use Color,” the Belvedere-Tiburon Library’s next art show.

The exhibit opens Nov. 19 with an artists’ reception from 6 to 7:30 p.m. and runs through Jan. 13. Because color is usually the first thing viewers notice in a painting, the library’s art committee asked Bay Area artists to submit pieces that show how they work with color. Pedersen’s painting will hang alongside works by Redwood City painter Linda Manes Goodwin, Oakland photographer Thomas Winz and Palo Alto painter Yuliya Krupnik.

item.title: Larry Stotter, Tiburon family-law attorney and title-winning masters athlete
item.description: Tiburon resident Larry Stotter argued a child-support case before the U.S. Supreme Court and in his 80s set masters track-and-field records. He died Oct. 25 at 97.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon resident Larry Stotter, a family-law attorney who argued a child-support case before the U.S. Supreme Court and in his 80s set masters track-and-field records, died of natural causes Oct. 25 at his Tiburon home. He was 97.

Stotter chaired the American Bar Association’s family-law section and in 2010 received its first-ever Legal Legend Award during the association’s annual meeting in San Francisco. He was also the first editor-in-chief of the section’s magazine, Family Advocate.

In 1978, he argued Kulko v. Superior Court before the U.S. Supreme Court on behalf of Ezra Kulko, a New York father whose former wife had sued him for child support in California. The court ruled for Kulko, holding that letting his daughter move to California did not subject him to the state’s courts.

Stotter was interviewed by The New York Times on family-law matters and wrote articles on the subject, culminating in his 2011 book “To Put Asunder: The Laws of Matrimonial Strife,” which traces two millenniums of marriage and relationship law.

“My goal is to break ground and provide starting points for the lawyer, researcher and legal historian concerned with the legal lore of the family,” he wrote in the book’s introduction as part of an effort “to help piece together the untold story of the written history of Anglo-American family law.”

Late in life, Stotter returned to track and field, a sport he had left as a teenager, and became the top U.S. decathlete among athletes ages 85-89 and No. 5 in the world, The Ark reported in 2017.

On July 16, 2017, he ran the lead leg on a 4x100-meter relay team that set a U.S. record of 2 minutes, 1.47 seconds for men 85 and older at the USA Track & Field Masters Outdoor Championships in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. The record still stands, according to USA Track & Field’s masters records.

Lawrence Henry Stotter was born Sept. 24, 1929, in Cleveland, the only child of Oscar and Bertha Stotter. At Cleveland Heights High School, he lettered in track and field and ran hurdles, he told The Ark in 2017, but he hung up his cleats in 1947.

Not long after, Stotter joined the U.S. Army as a commissioned second lieutenant. He fought in the Korean War and later took part in Operation Upshot-Knothole, the 11 nuclear test shots conducted in 1953 at the Nevada Test Site.

“At the time, of course, the health effects and environmental effects were not fully known, so he was very excited to watch a nuclear bomb exploding nearby and above his head,” said son Daniel “Dan” Stotter.

After his military service, Stotter attended Ohio State University on the GI Bill, earning a bachelor’s in commerce in 1956 and a law degree in 1958. Two years later, he was admitted to the California bar, where he remained an active member until 2005.

As an undergraduate, Stotter was a member of the Bucket and Dipper junior honorary society, the student court, the sailing club and the forensic society. As a law student, he was vice president of his class cabinet, an associate editor of the school’s law journal and an associate justice on its moot court.

Stotter practiced in other areas, such as patent law, but turned to family law in the 1960s after starting his own firm. He “really caught the early time period of family law becoming a very major area of law in California, especially,” his son said.

Dan Stotter, an environmental attorney, said his father cared most about protecting children, particularly from abduction, such as when a parent without custody takes a child from the parent with custodial rights.

Stotter worked to strengthen interstate child-abduction laws so that court orders returning children to their rightful custodians could be enforced, Dan Stotter said. In 1980, Stotter was a U.S. delegate to the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, a treaty meant to speed the return of a child wrongfully taken to another country. It has 103 parties.

“His legacy was caring about children,” Dan Stotter said of his father. “In the world of divorce, people do fight over money and children, and my father especially was known for his compassion for the family aspect of making sure that the children were taken care of after the divorce in a way that was appropriate.”

Between his undergraduate and law degrees, Stotter married fellow Ohio State student Ruth Rapoport in 1957. After time in San Francisco and Corte Madera, the couple moved in the 1960s to Tiburon’s Lyford Cove neighborhood, where they raised three children, Dan, Jennifer and Steven, all of whom attended Reed Union School District schools.

Daughter Jennifer Koran said her father “was just a people person” who put others at ease.

“He would walk in the room and walk out with five friends,” Koran said. “People just liked him and he liked people and being social.”

Outside his legal career, Koran and Dan Stotter said, their father took weaving classes, and some of his pieces hang on the walls of the family home. He also cooked, read, hiked and traveled. He collected Christmas Seals from boyhood and showed the collection in a free exhibit at the former Custom House in 2010, The Ark reported.

He and his wife floated down the Dordogne River in France, Koran said. Dan Stotter said his father was a docent on Angel Island and was active in the Tamalpais Conservation Club, including a stint as its chair. He also volunteered at the Friends of the Belvedere-Tiburon Library bookstore and played croquet with the Oakland, Mission Hills and Sonoma-Cutrer clubs, according to the family.

Stotter even drafted an autobiographical obituary, which Koran found while going through his belongings, she said.

“He wasn’t a right brainer or a left brainer,” Koran said. “He was everything.”

Stotter returned to track at the urging of Dan Stotter, who lives in Eugene, Oregon, a city nicknamed TrackTown USA.

When the two attended a meet at Hayward Field, the University of Oregon’s track-and-field stadium, Dan Stotter noticed his father had no trouble climbing to the top of the stairs while younger spectators in their 50s and 60s complained.

At his first event, the 2015 Hayward Classic, Stotter won two of the three throwing events he entered and the 100-meter dash for athletes 85 and older. At the 2017 Hayward Classic, he won gold medals in six events and silver in a seventh. In 2016, he and Dan Stotter each won decathlon gold medals in their age groups at the USA Track & Field Western Region championships at the College of Marin.

The masters world rankings announced at the 2017 Hayward Classic put him fifth, The Ark reported, and Dan Stotter said he was amazed by his father’s ability “to have the endurance at 85 to do five events one day and five events the second day.”

Stotter told The Ark in 2017 that he trained diligently because he wanted to test his limits.

“It’s the competition with myself,” Stotter said. “That’s the point. Say you can throw the javelin 13 meters, and 14 meters means you’ve reached a certain standard. Well, by God, then I’d like to do that.”

Koran said her father loved his family and “embraced life openheartedly.”

“Even people who’ve recently met him through my mom, they resonate with him,” Koran said. “He feels good to be around.”

Stotter is survived by his wife, Ruth Stotter; his children, Jennifer Koran, Dan Stotter and Steven Stotter; and his grandchildren, Benjamin Burress-Irving and Mia Koran.

Memorial services will be announced later, Dan Stotter said, but a celebration of life will be planned locally. The family has not designated a charity, but Dan Stotter said the Belvedere-Tiburon Library and the Tamalpais Conservation Club are organizations “that would be very supported by my father in donations.”

item.title: First of three Bay Area storms arrives Friday with rain, gusts and flood-prone tide
item.description: A coastal flood advisory covers the Tiburon Peninsula shoreline until 4 p.m. Nov. 13 as the first of three storms brings rain and gusts that could top 45 mph.
item.content:encoded:
A coastal flood advisory covers the Tiburon Peninsula shoreline until 4 p.m. Nov. 13 as the first of three storms brings rain and gusts that could top 45 mph.

The midday high tide Nov. 13 could flood Tiburon’s lowest shoreline streets just as the first of three storms forecast over the next week reaches the Bay Area with rain, gusts that could top 45 mph and a chance of thunderstorms.

The National Weather Service’s coastal flood advisory for the bay shoreline, including Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry, runs until 4 p.m. Nov. 13 and warns of up to 1.5 feet of water in low-lying areas.

NOAA tide predictions and recent gauge readings put that high tide off Tiburon at about 1:15 p.m., when water could reach Greenwood Beach Road and Tiburon Boulevard at Beach Road. The Beach Road intersection flooded Oct. 11 on a dry day.

The tide could test the wooden “tide boxes” Tiburon Public Works crews built over downtown storm drains to keep bay water from backing up onto the streets. The town has said crews pull the boxes whenever it rains so the drains can carry runoff, and residents should then expect flooding in those spots depending on rainfall and tides.

Rain is forecast to pick up across the North Bay from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. Nov. 13, with up to 1.25 inches in its coastal hills and 0.3-0.8 inch around San Francisco Bay by the afternoon of Nov. 14. Southerly gusts of 25-35 mph the night of Nov. 12 could top 45 mph just ahead of the cold front, strong enough to down trees and knock out power in spots, according to the weather service.

Boaters on the bay north of the Bay Bridge face a small craft advisory from 9 p.m. Nov. 12 to 9 a.m. 13, then a gale warning until 3 p.m.

Two more storms follow, Nov. 15-16 and again around the middle of next week, though forecasters don’t expect either to stall over one area, and early forecasts don’t show either bringing much more rain than the first.

The weekend’s big-surf warnings cover the Pacific coast from Point Reyes south through San Francisco and Monterey Bay to Big Sur, where breaking waves of 25 to 35 feet are forecast from the evening of Nov. 13 to early Nov. 15, with occasional 40- to 50-foot sets at some breaks. Waves could also wash over seawalls and run up beaches into low-lying areas Nov. 14, and the weather service calls the risk of drowning very high.

item.content:encoded:
Tiburon Public Works crews built wooden tide boxes over downtown storm drains to keep high tides from backing up onto Beach Road and other low-lying streets.

Tiburon Public Works crews have built wooden “tide boxes” over storm drains at low-lying downtown intersections to keep high tides from backing up onto the streets.

The boxes sit at Beach Road’s intersections with Tiburon Boulevard and Juanita Lane and at other spots that flood at high tide, according to a Nov. 2 town newsletter.

Each box sits over a drain. As the tide rises and pushes bay water up through the pipes, the box traps it and keeps it out of the street. The water recedes as the tide falls, the newsletter said. Crews seal the seams and hold each box down with weighted bags.

Tiburon will pay property owners up to half the cost, capped at $25,000, to fix failing private culverts and storm-drain pipes whose collapse could flood streets, damage town infrastructure or threaten public safety.

The Town Council approved the 12-month pilot program unanimously on Nov. 4. The program sets aside $100,000 and also covers catch basins, energy dissipators, drainage channels and other drainage structures approved by the Public Works Department.

Individual owners, neighbors applying jointly, homeowners associations, common-interest developments and other private owners can apply, and every owner of record must sign. The town will take applications for 12 months, and each approved project then has 12 months to finish.

item.title: Richardson Bay Sanitary District incumbents win new terms
item.description: Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens will keep their Richardson Bay Sanitary District seats over challenger John Turnacliff.
item.content:encoded:
Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens will keep their Richardson Bay Sanitary District seats over challenger John Turnacliff.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens will win new four-year terms on the Richardson Bay Sanitary District board, holding off challenger John Turnacliff in the count the county posted Nov. 9. The three would serve through November 2030, joining sitting board members Mark Slater and Jeff Slavitz.

Fitzgerald had votes on 47.4% of ballots counted, McIntosh on 46.2%, Walravens on 45.8% and Turnacliff on 19% in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9. Voters could choose up to three candidates, so the shares add up to more than 100%.

When those returns posted, 91,634 ballots had been counted countywide, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The results are unofficial. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16 and gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over a missing or mismatched signature, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix the problem.

The district’s first contested election since 2018 came amid renewed debate over whether Marin’s sanitary districts should consolidate. The board voted unanimously July 21 to reject all seven findings and nine recommendations in a Marin civil grand jury report that urged special districts to explore consolidation. District officials argued that the report failed to account for existing joint operations or the financial risks of merging.

The incumbents largely defended the district’s operations during preelection interviews with The Ark. Fitzgerald, a Tiburon Fire Protection District captain and the son of Ark contract bookkeeper Marion Fitzgerald and her husband, Jim, emphasized preparing for staff turnover and maintaining fiscal discipline.

McIntosh, the board president and co-founder of environmental-sensor company EnviroSmarts, stressed keeping sewer-service charges low and maintaining regional partnerships.

Walravens, a financial analyst and former attorney, pointed to financial stewardship and support for maintenance and capital improvements. All three said they doubted consolidation would improve the district’s service or finances, and Mark Fitzgerald and Walravens left room to consider specific efficiencies.

Turnacliff, who owns Golden Gate Equipment Finance and chairs the Marin County Republican Central Committee, said he would bring experience in financing, equipment planning and financial oversight. He said he was open to studying consolidation if it made financial and operational sense.

The district serves northern Tiburon from Gilmartin Drive to Highway 101 and all of Strawberry. It collects wastewater and pumps it to Mill Valley for treatment through the Sewerage Agency of Southern Marin.

The election was Fitzgerald’s first appearance on the ballot after more than four years on the board.

“For it to come to the voters and choose me amongst the other two, I’m thankful,” he said.

Looking ahead, Fitzgerald said his role includes overseeing how the district manages current spending and plans for future expenses.

“That’s what I care most about is that they plan for the future, spend money wisely currently and forecast the future cost,” he said.

Fitzgerald also praised McIntosh’s leadership as board president and said the board would revisit its officer assignments.

“Future outlook is just keep running a good agency,” he said.

McIntosh said the board’s work in the coming months would be routine, with no major votes scheduled. The district will review its accounting and business practices as it closes out the year, he said.

“It literally is business as usual,” McIntosh said. “We just kind of check everything to make sure we’re on track and we’re staying at or below budget.”

Turnacliff said in an email that the race was his first run for public office and that he thanked the voters who supported him.

“I’m a little disappointed, but I’m glad I ran and congratulations to the winners,” he said.

He said he plans to run again, “maybe for this seat, maybe another.”

item.title: Saghezchi, Waterfield, Teese keep Strawberry Rec board seats
item.description: Incumbents Sohrab Saghezchi, Sarah Waterfield and Peter Teese will win four-year Strawberry Recreation District seats over challenger David Morgenthaler.
item.content:encoded:
Incumbents Sohrab Saghezchi, Sarah Waterfield and Peter Teese will win four-year Strawberry Recreation District seats over challenger David Morgenthaler.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Incumbents Sohrab Saghezchi, Sarah Waterfield and board Chair Peter Teese will win the three four-year seats on the Strawberry Recreation District board, holding off challenger David Morgenthaler in the count the county posted Nov. 9.

Waterfield did not publicly campaign or sit for an interview, and in an email she declined to say whether she would take the seat.

Saghezchi had votes on 44.6% of ballots counted, Waterfield on 42.2%, Teese on 36.5% and Morgenthaler on 32.1% in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9. Voters could choose up to three candidates, so the shares add up to more than 100%.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

In a separate race for the board’s one two-year seat, appointed incumbent Doug Twillman is projected to win, with 65.9% of the vote to challenger Aliza Hawkins’ 34.1%.

When the Nov. 9 returns posted, 91,634 ballots had been counted countywide, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. The results are unofficial. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16 and gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over a missing or mismatched signature, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix the problem.

Morgenthaler, a Strawberry resident, mounted a rare challenge in a district that often struggles to draw candidates. Teese was elected without opposition in 2014, 2018 and 2022.

Teese, a board member since December 2010, sought a fifth term. Saghezchi, a Mill Valley dentist whom county supervisors appointed in December 2022 after no one filed for the seat, sought election to it for the first time. Waterfield joined the board in December 2024 after running uncontested for a shortened two-year term.

Morgenthaler, a sales professional and musician, campaigned on expanding programs for teenagers and adding offerings such as foreign-language and music classes. Saghezchi emphasized transparency, fiscal responsibility and community involvement, while Teese said his top priority was completing the district’s planned playground.

The incoming board will oversee a district serving about 6,000 residents in unincorporated Strawberry, with year-round recreation programs, classes, memberships and events.

Among its major projects is a playground planned for the grass between the tennis courts and baseball fields at Strawberry Park. The contractor, GameTime, trimmed the design to about $2.55 million in October, restroom included, and the board scheduled a final vote for Nov. 10, after The Ark’s press deadline. The district plans to break ground in 2027.

Saghezchi said he was “thrilled and honored” to continue serving the community and grateful for Strawberry residents’ support. He said he saw the results as an encouraging sign that residents recognized the board’s work.

Looking ahead to 2027, Saghezchi said he wants to continue improving the district’s facilities and programs and find more ways to bring residents together.

“Strawberry is a magical place, and I’m incredibly proud to call it home,” he said.

Teese said he was grateful, though he found it difficult to draw broader conclusions from the results beyond what he saw as an advantage for incumbents.

“I was happy to be in the top three,” he said.

“It’s a funny and odd reminder of democracy at work,” Teese said of seeing voters assign a number to each candidate.

He said a fifth term would be his last. The district has no term limits. The board voted unanimously Aug. 18 to reject a Marin civil grand jury recommendation that special districts cap members at two consecutive four-year terms.

Teese said the playground project would require a separate bidding process for site excavation, rather than handling that work and the playground equipment as a single package, and that the board would take up the excavation bidding Nov. 10.

Teese characterized the additional bidding requirement as an added step, not a complication, but expressed frustration with the government procedures involved in moving the project forward.

“Just to do a community good,” he said, “the legal hurdles that you face from your own team are astonishing.”

“I feel great about the playground, and I feel like an underdog when it comes to being up against red tape and bureaucracy and just the inertia of the state,” he said.

Morgenthaler said he expected the three incumbents to win reelection, though he stopped short of conceding as votes continued to be counted.

“I expect that the three incumbents will be reelected,” he said. “That’s my expectation at this point.”

Morgenthaler, who was making his first run for the board, called the current board “very capable” and said he planned to keep attending meetings. He also expressed interest in seeking an appointment if a seat opens before the next election.

“In the event that there is a vacancy in between now and the next cycle, I anticipate that I will show up and raise my hand,” he said.

Morgenthaler said he was “somewhat better than cautiously optimistic” about the district’s planned playground and would keep following its fundraising progress.

“I am very optimistic that the playground will be a wonderful way of expanding (the district’s) reach across the entire community,” he said.

item.title: Twillman projected to keep two-year Strawberry Rec board seat
item.description: Appointed incumbent Doug Twillman had 65.9% of the vote to Aliza Hawkins’ 34.1% for a two-year Strawberry Recreation District seat in the Nov. 9 count.
item.content:encoded:
Appointed incumbent Doug Twillman had 65.9% of the vote to Aliza Hawkins’ 34.1% for a two-year Strawberry Recreation District seat in the Nov. 9 count.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Appointed incumbent Doug Twillman is projected to win a two-year seat on the Strawberry Recreation District board, taking about two-thirds of the vote in the count the county posted Nov. 9 against challenger Aliza Hawkins, who sought the same seat by appointment last year.

Twillman had 65.9% of the vote to Hawkins’ 34.1% in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9, when 91,634 ballots had been counted countywide, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters.

The results are unofficial.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16 and gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over a missing or mismatched signature, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix the problem.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Twillman said his focus now is making sure the district builds its major new playground, slated for 2027.

“I’m excited, but I’ve never run in the interest of being popular,” he said. “I got a lot of eyes on me to make sure we get the playground done right.”

Hawkins did not respond to requests for comment.

The candidates competed for a single two-year seat in a rare contested election for a district that has historically struggled to attract candidates. Their campaigns emphasized community engagement, financial oversight and the future of the district’s planned playground.

Twillman joined the board in September 2025, when members selected him over Hawkins on a 3-1 vote to replace Cale Nichols, who had moved out of state. Board member Sohrab Saghezchi cast the dissenting vote, favoring Hawkins. The election put that choice before voters.

A financial analyst and consultant with more than 30 years of experience, Twillman emphasized fiscal oversight and completing the playground at Strawberry Park. He serves on the board’s fundraising committee for the project and called for dependable cost estimates before construction commitments.

“The budget should be well understood so that we can hold the contractors accountable and the community can hold us accountable for a successful physical and fiscal outcome,” Twillman said during the campaign.

Hawkins, whose background includes marketing, advertising and counseling, focused on increasing participation in district programs and helping residents feel included and represented.

“I would love to see more community engagement as well, just even letting people know more of what we have going on,” Hawkins said during the campaign.

A mother of two whose family regularly uses the district’s pool, programs and recreation facilities, Hawkins said she wanted the district to serve residents at every stage of life.

Playground company GameTime trimmed the design to about $2.55 million in October, restroom included. The board scheduled a final vote for Nov. 10, after The Ark’s press deadline. The district plans to break ground in 2027.

Established in 1949, the independent district serves about 6,000 residents in unincorporated areas of Mill Valley and Tiburon east of Highway 101. It operates the recreation center and maintains four parks, a public dock, walking trails and the Water Tank Hill open space.

item.title: Paradise Cay’s Measure Z dredging tax extension set to pass
item.description: Paradise Cay’s Measure Z, extending the parcel tax that pays to dredge its canals and channels, had 84.1% support in the county’s Nov. 9 count.
item.content:encoded:
Paradise Cay’s Measure Z, extending the parcel tax that pays to dredge its canals and channels, had 84.1% support in the county’s Nov. 9 count.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Paradise Cay’s Measure Z is projected to pass, extending the special parcel tax that pays to dredge the community’s canals and the two channels connecting it to San Francisco Bay.

The measure won 116 votes, or 84.1%, to 22 votes, or 15.9%, in the Marin County Elections Department’s count posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9. It needed two-thirds of the votes cast to pass.

The results are unofficial. As of Nov. 9, the county had counted 91,634 ballots, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16 and gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over a missing or mismatched signature, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix the problem.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

“We’re of course relieved that it passed and still by a decent margin,” said Eric Lyons, who chairs the six-member advisory board of County Service Area No. 29, the county-run district that collects the tax. “But it’s a little disappointing that there were 21 members who voted no.”

Lyons said some voters may have objected to the $300 increase.

“Of course costs are always going up. But we didn’t hear any pushback from anybody about that really in our little surveys,” he said. “But there are some older folks in the neighborhood that probably just would love to avoid any additional taxes on their bill, but I think we just probably need a little better education on what it really means.”

He said the district needs to better explain that a “no” vote would end the tax rather than keep the previous rate. If the tax lapsed, the community would lose its dedicated source of dredging money, which Lyons has said keeps the canals clear for boating and recreation.

“Without a yes vote, we don’t collect any money anymore,” he said.

Paradise Cay was built along the Tiburon Peninsula as a waterfront community organized around a network of residential canals. Keeping those canals and the entrances to the bay navigable requires the periodic removal of sediment carried into the waterways.

The waterways were last dredged in 2020 and 2024, and the community typically needs dredging every four or five years, depending on how quickly sediment accumulates.

The next dredging project is tentatively expected in 2028, Lyons said. Depending on conditions, the district might be able to wait until 2029.

“Our forecast shows that should be sufficient for 4-5 year dredging episodes over the next 10 years, but the cost of dredging and associated ‘soft’ costs (permits, planning and testing) has been rising rapidly, so we can only hope,” he said in September.

The 2024 project cost more than $1 million, including permits, planning, testing and other soft costs, Lyons said.

Measure Z would raise the tax in the service area from $1,900 per lot this year to $2,200 beginning July 1, 2027. The rate would rise automatically by 3% each year starting July 1, 2028, and the tax would expire June 30, 2037. With those increases, it would reach about $2,870 a lot in its final year.

The service area estimates the measure would raise an average of about $272,800 a year for maintenance dredging in Paradise Cay’s principal waterways and the north and south entry channels. The tax applies to lots in the district, which covers the Paradise Cay parcels with canal access rather than the whole neighborhood. The money may be used only for the purposes stated in the measure.

Measure Z would continue the existing parcel tax, which is scheduled to expire June 30, 2027. The current tax is Paradise Cay’s 2016 Measure O, which voters approved with 87.2% of the vote. It set a $1,500 annual parcel tax that could rise as much as 3% a year, to a maximum of $1,950 by 2026.

Measure O replaced a $1,200 annual parcel tax that 93.8% of voters approved in 2007. Measure Z’s 84.1% is the lowest yes vote of the three.

item.title: Elward projected to win Assembly seat; billionaire tax trails
item.description: Jackie Elward is projected to beat Supervisor Eric Lucan for the peninsula’s Assembly seat, while the billionaire tax trailed statewide and locally.
item.content:encoded:
Jackie Elward is projected to beat Supervisor Eric Lucan for the peninsula’s Assembly seat, while the billionaire tax trailed statewide and locally.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Rohnert Park Councilmember Jackie Elward is projected to win the Assembly seat representing the peninsula over Marin Supervisor Eric Lucan, while a one-time tax on billionaires trailed statewide and by even wider margins in Tiburon and Belvedere.

At the top of the ballot, Democrat Xavier Becerra will win the race for governor over Republican Steve Hilton, with a nearly 2-1 majority.

All results are unofficial and will change. The secretary of state’s 2:21 p.m. Nov. 9 update showed all 23,860 of the state’s precincts reporting, but Marin and other counties are still counting ballots.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

Marin’s Nov. 9 update counted 91,634 ballots, about 52.7% of the county’s 173,804 registered voters. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16.

Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25, and state law gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

On the peninsula, the county had counted ballots from 3,838 of Tiburon’s 7,553 registered voters, or 50.8%; 785 of Belvedere’s 1,618, or 48.5%; and 1,615 of Strawberry’s 3,081, or 52.4%. Peninsula figures are The Ark’s tallies of the precincts serving Belvedere, Strawberry and Tiburon, including unincorporated Tiburon areas such as Paradise Cay.

Results for the local council, school and district races and Paradise Cay’s Measure Z run in separate stories.

Special district, Strawberry and northern Tiburon voters

All four incumbents will win the four seats on the Southern Marin Fire Protection District board: Cristine Soto DeBerry with votes on 46.2% of ballots counted, Kurt Chun with 44.5%, Thomas Perazzo with 38.4% and Peter Fleming of Strawberry with 37.4%. Challengers Eric Steinhofer, 26.3%; Amy Svendberg, 24.7%; and Thomas Clark, 7.2%, trailed.

Belvedere Councilmembers Jane Cooper and Peter Mark, the only candidates for two seats, had votes on 71.5% and 63.3% of ballots counted. Incumbents also ran unopposed for three other boards: Joy Ho, Rick Jones and Cheryl Woodford on the Tiburon Fire Protection District board; Catharine Benediktsson and Tod Moody on the Sanitary District No. 5 of Marin board; and Natalie Katz, Sharon Nakatani and Yunhee Yoo on the board of the Mill Valley School District, which serves Strawberry Point Elementary School.

Ho, Woodford and Jones are scheduled to take the oath of office at the Tiburon Fire board’s meeting at 4 Nov. 11.

Marin County and Marin Healthcare District special taxes, all voters; each qualified by petition and needs a simple majority

Measure CC, the Marin Healthcare District’s 30-year parcel tax of 14 cents per square foot of building space for intensive care, trauma, emergency and other hospital capacity, will pass with 56.7%. It led in all three peninsula communities, with 53.8% in Tiburon, 51.4% in Belvedere and 56.5% in Strawberry.

The district estimates the tax will raise about $12.4 million a year to expand and modernize intensive care, trauma, triage and patient rooms at MarinHealth Medical Center and to hire and keep doctors and nurses. None of it can go to administrators’ salaries. It has no exemption for seniors or low-income owners, and the district may borrow against it. Opponents noted that district taxpayers are still paying off the $394 million hospital bond voters approved in 2013.

Measure P, the county’s 15-year childcare parcel tax of 5 cents per square foot, is projected to pass with 54.2%, though Tiburon voted against it 52.7% to 47.3% and Belvedere 55.7% to 44.3%. Strawberry backed it with 54.8%.

The county estimates the tax will raise about $12.5 million a year for childcare and preschool for low- and middle-income families, raises for childcare workers and new or improved childcare facilities, with no more than 5% for administration. The Marin County Children and Families Commission will write a five-year spending plan, and supervisors may raise the rate each year with inflation. Like Measure CC, it has no exemption for seniors or low-income owners.

Federal and state officials, district voters

Elward is projected to win the race to succeed Assemblymember Damon Connolly, D-San Rafael, in the 12th Assembly District, leading Lucan 56.6% to 43.4% with all 301 of its precincts reporting. Elward also led in Marin, 53.9% to 46.1%.

The peninsula went the other way. Lucan carried Tiburon with 56.5% and Belvedere with 64.3%, while Elward took Strawberry, 53.8% to 46.2%.

Connolly will win the open 2nd District state Senate seat over Republican Tief Gibbs of Novato, leading 74.7% to 25.3%.

Rep. Jared Huffman, D-San Rafael, will win reelection over Republican Robin Littau of Redding, leading 64.6% to 35.4% across the 2nd Congressional District. He took 82.9% in Marin.

State officials, all voters

Becerra will win with 65.6% to Hilton’s 34.4% in the secretary of state’s Nov. 9 count. He took 79.7% in Marin, 69.8% in Tiburon, 64.2% in Belvedere and 78% in Strawberry. Hilton, a former Fox News host from Atherton, ran best on the peninsula in Belvedere, at 35.8%.

Democrats will win the other partisan statewide races by similar margins: Treasurer Fiona Ma over Republican Gloria Romero for lieutenant governor, 65.5% to 34.5%; Secretary of State Shirley Weber over Republican Don Wagner, 66.5% to 33.5%; Controller Malia Cohen over Republican Herb Morgan, 65.5% to 34.5%; Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis over Republican Jennifer Hawks for treasurer, 65.7% to 34.3%; and Attorney General Rob Bonta over Republican Michael Gates, 65.5% to 34.5%.

The closest statewide race, for insurance commissioner, pitted two Democrats. Jane Kim is projected to win over state Sen. Ben Allen, leading 53.5% to 46.5%. Allen carried Marin with 56.3% and ran stronger still on the peninsula, with 64.5% in Tiburon, 68.8% in Belvedere and 62.1% in Strawberry.

In the nonpartisan race for superintendent of public instruction, San Diego Unified board President Richard Barrera will win over Chino Valley Unified board President Sonja Shaw, leading 58.9% to 41.1%. Barrera took 69.4% in Marin, 61.7% in Tiburon, 59.7% in Belvedere and 68.2% in Strawberry.

For the Board of Equalization’s District 2 seat, incumbent Sally Lieber will win over fellow Democrat John Pimentel, leading 59.9% to 40.1%.

All voters; each needs a simple majority

Proposition 40, the one-time 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026, trailed with 53.2% voting no statewide and 53.9% no in Marin. Tiburon voted against it 68.2% to 31.8% and Belvedere 77.8% to 22.2%. Strawberry opposed it 57.1% to 42.9%.

Proposition 42, one of two measures written to block it, led 52% to 48%. It would bar new state taxes on owning retirement accounts, financial assets and other personal property. Tiburon and Belvedere backed it, and Marin and Strawberry opposed it.

The other, Proposition 41, is projected to fail, trailing 45.4% to 54.6%. It would bar collecting any new tax that, like Proposition 40’s revenue, is exempt from the state spending limit. Belvedere backed it 56.3% to 43.7%, and Tiburon narrowly opposed it, 50.4% to 49.6%.

Proposition 3, which would make permanent the top income-tax brackets voters approved in 2012 and extended in 2016, will pass. It led 60.4% to 39.6% statewide and drew 67.3% in Marin. Tiburon narrowly opposed it, 51.6% to 48.4%, and Belvedere voted against it 59.5% to 40.5%. Strawberry backed it with 64.4%.

Proposition 5 is projected to pass, leading 51.9% to 48.1%, a margin of about 377,000 votes out of about 10 million. It would drop the replacement-candidate question from recall ballots and let the lieutenant governor succeed a recalled governor. Marin backed it with 58.9%, while Tiburon and Belvedere were narrowly against.

Proposition 38, the $8.4 billion immunology research bond, will pass. It had 54.3% statewide but trailed narrowly in Marin, 42,462 votes to 42,388, and in Tiburon and Belvedere.

Proposition 4, the closest measure on the ballot, would lift the state’s ban on public financing of campaigns. It trailed 49.6% to 50.4%, though Marin backed it with 56.4%.

Proposition 1, the $11.25 billion housing and veterans bond, passed with 60.9% to 39.1% and drew 68.4% in Marin. Proposition 2, which would double the cap on the state’s rainy-day fund, also passed. It had 61.2% and drew 73% in Marin. Proposition 37, the middle-income homebuyer loan program, passed with 62.2% and drew 65.2% in Marin.

Proposition 39, requiring voter ID, failed. It trailed 39.6% to 60.4%, and 76.5% of Marin voters opposed it. Proposition 43, which would require two-thirds approval for citizen-initiated local special taxes starting Jan. 1, 2027, will fail, trailing 43% to 57%, with 65.5% of Marin voters opposed.

Proposition 44, requiring community health clinics to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient care, failed. It trailed 17.9% to 82.1%, and 86.6% of Marin voters opposed it. Proposition 45, a faster environmental-review track for housing, infrastructure and other projects, is projected to fail, trailing 44.1% to 55.9%, and 71.4% of Marin voters opposed it.

California Supreme Court Associate Justices Kelli Evans and Joshua Groban will win retention to new 12-year terms, with 72.5% and 71.5% voting yes statewide.
