item.description: Krupa Antani leads Lina Godfrey by 54 votes for the third Reed Union School District seat, with only 1,515 challenged ballots countywide left to resolve.
item.content:encoded:
Krupa Antani leads Lina Godfrey by 54 votes for the third Reed Union School District seat, with only 1,515 challenged ballots countywide left to resolve.

By Kevin Hessel · Updated Nov. 20

UPDATE, Nov. 20: Krupa Antani’s lead over Lina Godfrey for the third Reed Union School District board seat narrowed to 54 votes in the Marin County count posted at 3:26 p.m. Nov. 20, down from 60 on Nov. 13.

Antani has 2,723 votes to Godfrey’s 2,669. Mike Ghaffary, with 3,751 votes, and Shelby Pasarell Tsai, with 3,534, remain on track for the other two seats.

The county reports no ballots left to count except 1,515 vote-by-mail ballots challenged for missing or non-matching signatures. Voters have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them, and the county says official final results will be published that day. The election must be certified by Dec. 3.

Countywide, 128,525 ballots have been counted, 74.0% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters.

By Kevin Hessel · Updated Nov. 13

UPDATE, Nov. 13: Krupa Antani widened her lead over Lina Godfrey for the third Reed Union School District board seat to 60 votes in the Marin County Elections Department’s count posted at 4:48 p.m. Nov. 13, up from 25 votes Nov. 11. Antani has 2,665 votes to Godfrey’s 2,605.

Mike Ghaffary, with 3,688 votes, and Shelby Pasarell Tsai, with 3,460, remain on track for the other two seats.

Countywide, 125,641 ballots have been counted, 72.3% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. The next county update is Nov. 17.

By Kevin Hessel · Updated Nov. 11

UPDATE, Nov. 11: Krupa Antani has moved 25 votes ahead of Lina Godfrey for the third seat on the Reed Union School District board in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 3:20 p.m. Nov. 11.

Antani had votes on 36.2% of ballots counted in the race, to Godfrey’s 35.8%, her first lead in four counts. Godfrey led on election night and by two votes Nov. 5, and the two were tied Nov. 9.

Antani and Godfrey remain tied among Tiburon voters, with 1,646 votes each. Antani’s margin comes from Belvedere, where she leads by 30 votes, while Godfrey leads by five in the Strawberry portion of the district.

The Ark projects that Mike Ghaffary, with votes on 49.9% of ballots, and Shelby Pasarell Tsai, with 46.6%, will win the other two seats.

The results are unofficial. The county’s next update is scheduled for Nov. 13.

The story below ran in the Nov. 11 print edition.

By Francisco Martinez · Nov. 3, 2026

Ghaffary, Pasarell Tsai will win Reed seats as Godfrey, Antani battle for third

Mike Ghaffary and Shelby Pasarell Tsai will win seats on the Reed Union School District board of trustees, while Lina Godfrey and fellow challenger Krupa Antani were tied for the third seat, with 1,864 votes each, in the count the county posted Nov. 9.

Ghaffary led the four-person field with votes on 49.8% of the ballots counted in the race in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9. Pasarell Tsai had votes on 47.2% of ballots. Godfrey and Antani each had votes on 35.7% of ballots.

Those results are unofficial. Countywide, 91,634 ballots had been counted as of Nov. 9, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. The county’s next updates are scheduled for Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25, and state law gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

If the race for the third seat ends in a tie, the winner will be chosen by lot, under a procedure the board set before the election as state law requires, according to the district.

The top three finishers will win four-year terms that end in 2030.

Ghaffary, a venture capitalist, was appointed to the board 4-0 at a special Feb. 6 meeting to fill the seat Sherry Wangenheim left when she resigned in December 2025 with a year left on her term. His appointed term runs through early December.

Pasarell Tsai, an attorney and the board president, won her first term in 2022. Board member Afsaneh Zolfaghari did not seek a third term, so Godfrey or Antani will join the board as its newcomer.

Godfrey is a Tiburon disability-access advocate on the town’s Diversity Inclusion Task Force. Antani is a former public-school teacher with three children in the district.

“I’m very thankful that so many voters seem that they want to return me and that I’m thankful for the support,” Pasarell Tsai said.

Godfrey acknowledged on election night that results were early and commended her fellow candidates for their campaigns, saying there were “four qualified candidates for these seats.”

“I’m hopeful that we had better turnout,” she said.

“I am grateful to all the students, parents, teachers and staff who work so hard in our school district every day. Thank you to our community for continuing to support our excellent Reed Union schools,” Ghaffary said.

“I think it’s important to let the process play out,” Antani said, adding that many mail-in ballots had yet to be counted.

“Every vote matters, which is what we’re seeing in this race … so I think I’m in the mindset that we need to focus on letting this play out and getting the results in,” she said.

She said she was proud of the race and of the support for the race and for Measure O, adding that she would continue volunteering at Reed schools regardless of the results because she enjoys it.

The board race was one of two decisions facing Reed Union voters. Residents in the district, which includes Tiburon, Belvedere and east Corte Madera, also voted on Measure O, a $115 million bond measure that would fund upgrades at all three district campuses and that The Ark projects will pass.

If the bond measure holds the 55% approval it needs, the winners of the board race will join their two other colleagues in overseeing how those funds are spent. The bond is just one issue facing the Reed district. Others include continuing efforts to challenge all students academically, to balance the district budget without sacrificing student programs and to look critically at how technology is used in the classroom.

The new board will also inherit a projected $1.2 million deficit in the district’s $34.5 million budget for 2026-2027, which trustees adopted unanimously June 8. The district’s forecast shows deficits of $1.5 million in each of the next two fiscal years, and by fiscal 2029 it would fall short of the board’s own reserve policy.

Ghaffary previously said his top priorities if elected would be encouraging the district to develop responsible guidelines around technology use in the classroom, ensuring the district continues to support and challenge all students academically and continuing to plan for the district’s long-term fiscal stability.

Pasarell Tsai previously said she was focused on increasing academic rigor for all students as part of her second term. She pointed to a change the district made beginning in the 2023-2024 school year to have all seventh-grade students take accelerated math as an example of how differentiated learning can be successful. She also highlighted the board’s need to balance its budget and support district staff in what’s a “very expensive cost-of-living area.”

Antani previously said her goals included making sure the district is following its 2024-2030 strategic plan. She noted that means focusing on the whole child, including academic rigor and social-emotional learning. She also said another priority was using the district’s Local Control Accountability Plan — a state-mandated document that requires districts to outline their priorities and track student progress — as a guide to better understand whether the funds being spent for interventions and academic programs are resulting in the desired outcomes.

Godfrey said she wanted to focus on providing Reed Union students with an academically rigorous experience and increase transparency in governance. She lobbied the board to stream its meetings on Zoom to allow more people to view sessions and wants to allow for live public comment for those watching remotely.

item.title: Teacher-backed challengers win all three Tam Union board seats
item.description: Valerie Wynn, Brian Sutherland and Joy Scully Koo will win three Tamalpais Union board seats, with board President Cynthia Roenisch running fifth.
item.content:encoded:
Valerie Wynn, Brian Sutherland and Joy Scully Koo will win three Tamalpais Union board seats, with board President Cynthia Roenisch running fifth.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Three Mill Valley challengers endorsed by the district’s teachers union will win the three Tamalpais Union High School District board seats on the ballot, based on returns the county posted Nov. 9, with board President Cynthia Roenisch running fifth.

Valerie Wynn, a retired district teacher, led the seven-candidate field with votes on 48.2% of ballots counted. Brian Sutherland, an appellate and constitutional lawyer, had votes on 45.4% of ballots, and Joy Scully Koo, an engineer with an MBA, on 36.7%, according to results Marin County elections officials posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9.

Former board President Leslie Harlander, a retired civil engineer, was fourth with votes on 21.2% of ballots, just ahead of Roenisch’s 19.8% and 15.5 percentage points behind Koo. Spanish teacher Maria Sandoval had 13.9%, and Kevin Saavedra, who resigned from the board Oct. 9, had 10.9%.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The results are unofficial. The Nov. 9 count included 91,634 ballots countywide, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16.

Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25, and state law gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

The district runs Redwood High School, the main public high school for Tiburon and Belvedere students, and Tamalpais High School, which serves Strawberry, along with Archie Williams High School in San Anselmo and two alternative schools. Board members are elected districtwide, so the race was on every peninsula ballot.

Taken together, peninsula voters put Sutherland first. In Tiburon’s precincts, he had votes on 41.6% of ballots to Wynn’s 39.6%, and in Belvedere 43.1% to her 36.3%. Strawberry voters put Wynn ahead, 43% to 39.9%.

Koo was third in all three communities, with 28.6% in Tiburon, 28.8% in Belvedere and 33.6% in Strawberry. Harlander ran fourth in Tiburon with 24.9%, and Roenisch was fourth in Belvedere with 20.9% and in Strawberry with 22.1%.

Ballots counted so far stood at 3,838 of 7,553 registered voters in Tiburon, 785 of 1,618 in Belvedere and 1,615 of 3,081 in Strawberry.

The third seat was open because board member Emily Uhlhorn did not seek reelection. She will finish her term and become executive director of the Tam High Foundation in January.

Saavedra stepped down the day after a judge granted a district parent a three-year civil harassment restraining order against him. His name stayed on the ballot, but he stopped campaigning and said he would not serve if elected.

Roenisch and Saavedra were first elected in 2018, the year the Marin County Office of Education ordered the district to produce a deficit-reduction plan and warned it could be insolvent as early as 2020.

Roenisch, a Corte Madera resident who teaches Advanced Placement English at Alameda High School, ran on experience, arguing at the League of Women Voters’ Sept. 28 forum that the district needed seasoned board members as budgets tighten. At a board meeting in October, parents faulted her for not publicly disciplining Saavedra, and at least one called on her to resign. She said she would not.

Most of the challengers campaigned on rebuilding trust after a string of 3-2 votes, including the June 2025 decision not to renew $250,000 in contracts with consultants who ran support programs for Black students at Tamalpais High and the April 14 bell-to-bell cellphone ban. Roenisch, Saavedra and board member Jennifer Holden formed the majority each time.

The teachers union and the Marin Democratic Party endorsed Koo, Sutherland and Wynn. A committee called Tam Union Governance Alliance supported the three while opposing Harlander, Saavedra and Roenisch, according to campaign-finance disclosures.

In the last reports before the election, covering Sept. 20 to Oct. 17, Harlander reported spending $16,010, Sutherland $8,204, Wynn $5,068 and Koo $4,786. No contributions or spending for Roenisch, Saavedra or Sandoval appeared in the county’s online filings.

The new board takes over a basic-aid district, funded mainly by local property taxes, whose enrollment fell from 5,146 students in 2020-2021 to 4,316 last school year. The district has made $3.57 million in staffing cuts since February 2025 to hold its reserves. Its Measure M parcel tax, now $560 a parcel and about 14% of a district budget of about $130 million, expires in June 2029.

The board’s minimum reserve is 17% of spending, but budget projections presented in March showed reserves dipping to about 15.5% this school year. Voters approved Measure B, a $289 million facilities bond, in 2024, eight months after a $517 million bond narrowly failed.

No Tam Union measure was on the Nov. 3 ballot. The board discussed in June whether to seek a renewal this fall but took no action before the Aug. 7 deadline. Wynn said at the forum that contract talks with the Tamalpais Federation of Teachers begin next year.

Members elected Nov. 3 take office Dec. 11, joining board members Holden and Ida Green, whose seats were not on the ballot.

item.title: Ryan, Hornbrook, Defever set to win Tiburon Town Council seats
item.description: Jack Ryan, Chuck Hornbrook and Kathleen Defever lead Faris Jafar and Alice Fredericks for three Tiburon Town Council seats in Marin’s Nov. 9 count.
item.content:encoded:
Jack Ryan, Chuck Hornbrook and Kathleen Defever lead Faris Jafar and Alice Fredericks for three Tiburon Town Council seats in Marin’s Nov. 9 count.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Jack Ryan, Chuck Hornbrook and Kathleen Defever will win the three Tiburon Town Council seats on the ballot, leading Faris Jafar and Alice Fredericks in the five-way race in the count the county posted Nov. 9.

Results as of 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9 showed Ryan leading the race with votes on 51.8% of ballots counted, followed by Hornbrook, on 51.5%, and Defever, on 43.4%. Jafar trailed with votes on 35.1% of ballots, and Fredericks had votes on 28.5%.

Because each voter could choose up to three candidates, the shares add up to more than 100%.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

Jafar and Fredericks both conceded election night.

The top three finishers will serve four-year terms until November 2030.

With Fredericks out and Mayor Jon Welner not seeking reelection, Hornbrook and Defever will join the council as its two newcomers.

The council typically accepts the certified results and rotates the mayor’s seat in December. In 2024, it accepted the results Dec. 4 and chose a new mayor the same night.

The results are unofficial. Countywide, 91,634 ballots had been counted as of Nov. 9, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16.

Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. The county’s next updates are scheduled for Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25, and state law gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Tiburon’s turnout was 84.9% in the 2024 presidential election and 71.4% in the 2022 midterm, according to certified results.

Ryan, the incumbent who first won a seat in a 2020 special election and a full term in 2022, said he was humbled by Tiburon voters’ choice in making him the leading vote-getter and looked forward to the new term.

“We’re going to have at least one new councilmember, and I’m excited to work with the new council in the new year,” he added.

Hornbrook, a Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission member who ran unsuccessfully in 2024, said he looked forward to addressing issues he heard on the campaign trail, estimating he knocked on some 900 doors. In a Nov. 6 statement to The Ark, he said he would focus on traffic, community vibrancy and town accountability.

He said he was excited to be “getting to work and helping deliver what the people of Tiburon want to get done.”

Defever, a Planning Commission member who ran unsuccessfully for the council in 2020 and 2021, said she had just seen the results when The Ark contacted her and was thrilled. The results were “something I’ve been looking forward to,” she said.

“I’m excited to have the voters’ support, and I cannot wait to get to work and get some of the issues I’ve heard about on the campaign trail addressed,” Defever said.

“I think Tiburon’s decided pretty decisively who they wanted, and I’m excited to work with everybody on all the initiatives we talked about during the campaign,” Jafar said. “To the extent that I can help with the policy initiatives we talked during the campaign, I’m happy to lend a hand.”

Fredericks, the longest-serving councilmember in Tiburon’s history, said she would now consider her next volunteer options.

“I would like to congratulate the people who now sit on the council,” Fredericks said. “It’s going to be very exciting.”

Ryan, Hornbrook and Defever will serve on a council facing calls for more financial transparency after delayed year-end audits and a budgeting process that did not include up-to-date actual spending figures from the prior year, including for the current fiscal year 2026-2027. All five candidates backed an independent finance committee like Belvedere’s.

Those financial concerns extend to new revenue sources. Town Manager Greg Chanis told councilmembers May 20 that Tiburon must explore how to pay for park improvements, a longstanding upgrade of the Public Works Department’s corporation yard and improvements identified in the town’s traffic study, adopted in May.

Housing remains a central issue. The state Department of Housing and Community Development can review Tiburon’s housing element at midcycle as soon as summer 2027, examining whether the town is following through on the housing programs it has committed to.

Tiburon was allocated 639 units as part of its 2023-2031 housing-element cycle. Although the town needs only to identify where the units can be built, falling short in the review could trigger consequences.

Town officials previously indicated the most severe consequences would make the town ineligible for state funding, expose it to sanctions from the state Attorney General’s Office and activate the “builder’s remedy,” under which developers could build regardless of local zoning restrictions.

At the center of the housing discussion is a 127-unit plan for three downtown Tiburon sites owned by A&C Ventures. The company announced the plan Oct. 22; its 127 units would cover nearly 20% of the town’s housing allocation.

The new council will also inherit unsettled questions on parks and police cameras. The town has not decided how to pay for a planned park at the former sanitation ponds site near McKegney Green, projected to cost $3.7 million to build, and the earliest voters could approve a tax or bond for it is November 2028.

All five candidates said they were open to a public hearing on the town’s Flock license-plate cameras, a debate that had not reached a council agenda as of Election Day.

Hornbrook, a vocal advocate for more fiscal transparency, has pledged to bring the creation of a finance committee to a council vote within his first 90 days in office. On town revenue, he wants to examine how the town spends its money and cut costs where needed before considering a bond measure or sales-tax increase.

On housing, Hornbrook supports talking with other agencies, such as the Reed Union School District, to explore workforce-housing solutions. He said the town should work with the state mandates as written; challenging them, he said, can result in even less local control.

Ryan also supports an independent finance committee to help the council analyze town revenues and expenditures and plan ahead. He said the town should communicate its finances better, and he has said the word “transparency” in a government context results in “an inference or an implication that something’s being hidden.”

Ryan said he wanted to plan the town’s long-term spending before deciding how to raise money, but he said raising the town’s sales tax by half a cent is an option to close gaps for projects. On housing, Ryan considered A&C Ventures’ efforts to have the greatest effect on how the town thinks about its housing element.

Defever also supports more financial transparency and said councilmembers should listen to residents who ask for more information. She said she wanted to examine the town budget more closely to figure out how Tiburon could add revenue sources, but she has said there are ways Tiburon can cut its spending, such as on litigation, before exploring new revenue.

Defever has criticized state housing mandates, describing their implementation as “one size fits all.” She previously said that while the town must follow state law, Tiburon should also “try to come up with some alternative strategies to maintain Tiburon for the beautiful attributes that it has.”

item.title: Reed district’s $115 million Measure O projected to pass
item.description: Measure O, Reed Union’s $115 million school bond, had 60.1% support in Marin’s Nov. 9 count, about 5 points above the 55% it needs to pass.
item.content:encoded:
Measure O, Reed Union’s $115 million school bond, had 60.1% support in Marin’s Nov. 9 count, about 5 points above the 55% it needs to pass.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

The Ark projects that voters in the Reed Union School District will pass a $115 million bond to repair and upgrade the district’s three schools, based on returns the county posted Nov. 9.

Measure O had 60.1% support in the county’s count, posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9, 2,871 votes to 1,908. That put it about 5 percentage points above the 55% it needs.

The results are unofficial. As of Nov. 9, the county had counted 91,634 ballots, about 52.7% of its 173,804 registered voters. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The next results updates are scheduled for Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. State law gives Marin County until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Reed Union board President Shelby Pasarell Tsai, who was also on the ballot for reelection, said on election night that “early returns look good” and that she was feeling “hopefully optimistic” for the district.

Pasarell Tsai said she was “really looking forward to community recognizing the importance of strong and vibrant schools, and it shows that our community really does value the schools.”

The tax would be levied on properties in the district, which includes Tiburon, Belvedere and east Corte Madera, beginning in fiscal year 2027-2028, when the district expects the rate to peak at $30 per $100,000 of assessed value. That works out to $300 a year for every $1 million of assessed value.

The district estimates the rate would average $26.63 per $100,000 over the life of the bonds, with the tax collected for the last time in fiscal 2060-2061. The levy would raise about $6.2 million a year, according to the ballot question, and the district’s tax rate statement estimates that repaying the full $115 million would cost $213 million in principal and interest.

Property owners in the district already pay a combined rate of about $21.60 per $100,000 of assessed value for two earlier Reed school bonds: a $38 million bond approved in 2001 that ends in 2028 and a $13 million bond that ends in 2031, according to district consultant Capital Finance Group.

The district’s current bond rate is the third lowest among 12 elementary school districts in Marin, according to figures presented to the board June 2. With Measure O, its rate would still fall in the middle range of comparable districts.

No argument against Measure O was filed with the Marin County Elections Department.

The district’s board voted unanimously June 8 to put the measure on the ballot. The district will set priorities for the money using its long-range facilities plan, begun in spring 2022 and completed in 2024 to guide building projects at the three campuses over the next 10-15 years.

Pasarell Tsai said before the election that $115 million falls short of the district’s needs and that the district has no intention of bringing a second bond measure to voters.

School districts in California usually turn to bond measures to pay for repairs, renovations and new construction because they receive no dedicated funding for facilities upkeep. A bond functions as a loan taken out by the school district that property owners pay back through increased property taxes.

No bond money can be used for teacher or administrator salaries, and the measure requires a citizens’ oversight committee and annual independent audits. The measure’s text also says the money must be spent on the district’s schools and cannot be taken by the state or county.

Needs across the district include replacing portable classrooms and installing air conditioning in all rooms on all three campuses.

Other districtwide work includes upgrading failing clay-pipe plumbing, repairing leaking roofs, removing asbestos and mold from aging buildings and making campuses more accessible than the Americans with Disabilities Act requires.

At Bel Aire Elementary School, identified improvements include installing heaters in three buildings, repaving the lower playground and creating shade for the lunch area.

At Reed Elementary School, other high-priority work includes replacing roofs over the administration building, building a covered lunch area and replacing old walkways.

And at Del Mar Middle School, improvements include repaving the playground, fixing concrete and asphalt, replacing stairs from the field to the street and redoing the track.

item.title: Tiburon’s Marilyn Nemzer wins new term on Marin Board of Education
item.description: Marilyn Nemzer had 70.3% of the vote over fellow Tiburon resident Avery Lieberman for the Marin County Board of Education seat covering the peninsula.
item.content:encoded:
Marilyn Nemzer had 70.3% of the vote over fellow Tiburon resident Avery Lieberman for the Marin County Board of Education seat covering the peninsula.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Tiburon resident Marilyn Nemzer will win another four years on the Marin County Board of Education over a challenger backed by one of her board colleagues.

Nemzer had 70.3% of the vote to 29.7% for challenger and fellow Tiburon resident Avery Lieberman in county results posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9, the latest available at The Ark’s press time.

The Trustee Area 5 seat covers all of Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry as well as Corte Madera and Larkspur. The Reed Union School District lies entirely within its boundaries. The winner will serve a four-year term ending in November 2030.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The results are unofficial. As of Nov. 9, the county had counted 91,634 ballots, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted.

The next results updates are scheduled for Nov. 11, as well as Nov. 13, 17, 20 and 25. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. State law gives Marin County until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Nemzer said on election night that she was relieved and happy with the early results and that being elected is a special feeling.

“I just love being involved in what we do on the board, and I’m just really, really happy that it looks like I will have a chance to continue,” Nemzer said in a phone interview.

Lieberman declined to comment on the results.

The Marin County Board of Education provides citizen oversight of educational programs and services run by the Marin County Office of Education. It works with the voter-elected county superintendent of schools to set county-office priorities.

Its duties include adopting or rejecting, but not modifying, the elected superintendent’s proposed budget; setting the superintendent’s salary; hearing appeals of student expulsions or denied interdistrict transfer requests; and maintaining positive relationships with the county’s 17 school districts.

Nemzer, 84, has represented the Tiburon Peninsula on the board since 2001 and sought a seventh term. Her key priorities include maintaining the county Office of Education’s long-term programs, including outdoor education at Walker Creek Ranch and Career Technical Education, and expanding collaboration among districts to share services and cut costs.

Lieberman, 65, a former assistant professor of dentistry, has lived in Tiburon for 31 years.

The race was the first contested election for the seat in at least 13 years. Nemzer was the only candidate to file in 2013, and no challenger emerged in 2018 or 2022.

Nemzer’s race became a proxy for existing tensions on the school board between her and board member Nancy McCarthy, who encouraged Lieberman to run and who has clashed repeatedly with her colleagues on the board.

Lieberman was one of three challengers seeking to unseat incumbents on the seven-member board, and he said McCarthy also recruited another of them, The Ark reported in September.

McCarthy — who has drawn criticism from her colleagues in recorded meetings, including claims that she has created a toxic environment during her tenure — financially supported a committee, Educate Our Children, that spent against Nemzer and fellow incumbent Curtis Robinson, who also sought reelection. Robinson will win his race to represent Sausalito and part of Mill Valley.

McCarthy has criticized Nemzer for accepting county-paid health benefits, which Lieberman said he would not accept if elected. Nemzer has defended the benefit, saying the option to receive health coverage allows people from lower-income backgrounds to seek the office.

Lieberman’s social-media posts have also drawn accusations of bigotry. He sued the University of California in November 2020, alleging he was laid off from his job as an assistant clinical professor at its San Francisco dental school and publicly branded a racist over posts on his personal Facebook page. The parties settled the suit in October 2024, with no admission of wrongdoing and no allegations tested at trial.

In one post, Lieberman wrote that saying “all lives matter” was “now considered to be the ‘go-to response from a racist.’” He also commented “So true!” on another user’s post invoking slavery, Jim Crow and reparations. Lieberman deleted the “all lives matter” post and apologized publicly after a colleague told him students had been hurt by it, according to his complaint. In a deposition, Lieberman acknowledged a reader could construe his agreement with the latter post as racist.

The dispute began in June 2020, days after George Floyd’s murder in Minneapolis. A student complained that Lieberman’s posts were offensive, according to court filings. A faculty member relayed the student’s words in an email quoted in the case: “Apparently this is how he feels about people of my skin color.” The student said Lieberman had since deleted “a lot of the racial posts.”

More recently, in April, Lieberman wrote Facebook posts directed at Muslims as a group.

In an April 19 post, Lieberman shared a Breitbart story headlined “North London Synagogue ‘Firebombed’ in Latest Anti-Jewish Attack.” Above the link he wrote: “For those of you who favor open borders and unelected judges (Obama appointees) who block efforts to deport violent hate filled Muslims.”

In an April 17 post, Lieberman shared a message from conservative commentator David J. Harris Jr. paraphrasing Catholic Bishop Athanasius Schneider: “They are not refugees, they are invaders who want to Islamize Europe. They want to destroy historical culture in Europe.” Harris asked, “Thoughts?” Lieberman answered, “And they’ve succeeded.”

In September, Lieberman defended the posts and said he was not referring to all Muslims.

“Most are peaceful and tolerant but a small percentage aren’t,” he wrote. Lieberman, who is Jewish, added that he was concerned about rising antisemitism worldwide and feels an obligation to speak up against attacks on Jews.

Lieberman said those who “try to label me as racist or hateful” over the posts should recognize that he has been a victim of hate himself. He said he would stand up for people of all races and religions.

“I support diversity, equity and inclusion, but only when applied to everyone, not just certain groups,” he wrote.
